title: Thomas Walker and Cumberland Gap
summary: In April 1750 Dr. Thomas Walker recorded Cave Gap on an Indian road through the Appalachians and named it for the Duke of Cumberland, now Cumberland Gap.
bodyMarkdown:
In the spring of 1750, Virginia physician and surveyor Thomas Walker led a small party across the mountains into what is now Kentucky. His journal is the first known written record of a colonial expedition through the gap later called Cumberland Gap. The land he crossed was Native country, laced with hunting paths and the remains of older towns.

## The Loyal Land Company

[Thomas Walker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Walker_(explorer)) says the Loyal Land Company was founded on July 12, 1749, with Walker as a leading member alongside Joshua Fry and Peter Jefferson. The company received a royal grant of 800,000 acres in what is now southeastern Kentucky, land then occupied by Native Americans. It sent Walker to explore and survey the region.

## Cave Gap

The [Grokipedia entry on Thomas Walker](https://grokipedia.com/page/Thomas_Walker_(explorer)) says the party left Castle's Woods, Virginia, on March 6, 1750. On April 13 Walker recorded passing through a notch in the mountains that he called Cave Gap, for a large cave and spring at its foot. The journal also notes coal outcrops, game trails and Cherokee hunting paths.

The pass was later renamed for Prince William Augustus, Duke of Cumberland. A later account by a son of Joseph Martin says Walker and others drank to the duke's health at the gap, giving rise to the name of the mountain and river.

## A cabin and a mound

Walker's party built a cabin in present Knox County, called the first non-Indian house in Kentucky. Grokipedia gives two different dates for it, April 7 and April 13, 1750. Walker is also credited as the first to find and use coal in Kentucky.

Later that month, Walker described "several Indian cabbins" and an artificial mound about 20 feet high. A [2000 Filson Club History Quarterly article](https://npshistory.com/publications/cuga/fchq-v74n4-2000.pdf) identifies that passage as an account of the Mississippian town now called the [Croley-Evans site](/stories/croley-evans-site/).

## Later career

Walker went on to serve in Virginia's House of Burgesses and to represent Virginia at the Treaty of Fort Stanwix and in talks with the Six Nations. He also surveyed the "Walker Line," which still forms much of the Kentucky–Tennessee border. He advised Thomas Jefferson on his Notes on the State of Virginia.

Grokipedia notes that Daniel Boone's 1775 improvements turned the route through the gap into the Wilderness Road. It says more than 200,000 migrants used it by 1810.

## Kentucky today

The [Dr. Thomas Walker State Historic Site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dr._Thomas_Walker_State_Historic_Site), six miles southeast of Barbourville, marks the area where he built his cabin. It displays a replica of the cabin. The [Grokipedia entry on Cumberland Gap](https://grokipedia.com/page/Cumberland_Gap) says the gap itself lies within Cumberland Gap National Historical Park, established by Congress in 1940.
